about_html:
The model of section 7 of Energy System Models answers one question: what should Denmark build for a decarbonised power system in 2050, and how should it run it, if everything is chosen to serve demand at the lowest total cost? It covers twelve bidding zones: Denmark's two (DK1 in the west, DK2 in the east), Germany, five Norwegian and four Swedish zones. Denmark is built from scratch; the neighbours keep the plants they have today and may build more beside them.

Chosen by the model Given to it
Plants and stores what Denmark builds: solar, onshore and offshore wind, gas plants and peakers (on natural gas or biomethane), nuclear, batteries of two, four or eight hours; and what the neighbours add from the same menu what each costs to build and run, fuel prices, a discount rate of 7 %, the land and sea available, the neighbours' plants of today
Operation how everything runs, in every part of the year the weather of one year, 2024 in the reference
Trade the flow over each interconnector today's interconnectors
Demand how much demand response is called on each zone's demand in 2050, hour by hour, and the willingness to pay of its flexible blocks
Carbon the emissions, which follow from all of the above a price of 85 € per tonne on every emitter in every zone

What it minimises, and what its prices mean. The total annual cost of the twelve-zone system: the annualised cost of what is built plus the cost of running it. A competitive market with these costs would reach the same outcome, so a zone's price in an hour reads as a market price: the cost of serving one more MWh there, set by whatever is at the margin, a plant, a battery, an import or demand response.

How time is handled. The year is cut into 1,095 chronological segments, short where things change fast and long where they do not; every quantity is weighted by the hours its segment stands for.

The scenarios. The reference case is solved, then solved again with one given changed at a time: the carbon price, fuel and technology costs, demand, what flexibility is available, the interconnectors, the land, the weather year and how finely time is resolved. Each scenario is a complete new optimum: everything the model chooses is chosen again, not adjusted from the reference.

What the candidates cost, as the reference case prices them. The annual fixed cost is the annuity at 7 % plus fixed operation and maintenance; the running cost is fuel and variable operation, and carbon at 85 €/t where the plant emits. A battery's fixed cost includes its energy.

Annual fixed cost, k€ per MW Running cost before carbon, €/MWh CO₂, t per MWh Running cost at 85 €/t, €/MWh
Solar 29.3 0.0 – 0.0
Onshore wind 94.1 1.3 – 1.3
Offshore wind 168.0 0.0 – 0.0
Nuclear 753.8 22.1 – 22.1
Gas, combined cycle 100.2 34.3 0.33 62.4
Gas, open cycle 45.3 46.8 0.46 85.9
Biomethane, open cycle 45.3 149.4 – 149.4
Battery, 2 hours 22.5
Battery, 4 hours 35.4
Battery, 8 hours 61.1

What the weather offers wind and solar in 2024: the full-load hours each could run if none of its output were curtailed, and the most each Danish zone may build. How much is built, and how many of those hours it runs, is the model's choice.

Hours offered in DK1 Hours offered in DK2 Potential in DK1, GW Potential in DK2, GW
Solar 910 982 10 6
Onshore wind 3,658 4,089 5 2.5
Offshore wind 4,713 4,632 20 10

Demand response, in every zone: blocks of demand that go unserved when the price exceeds their willingness to pay.

How much Willingness to pay
Flexible demand 5 % of the zone's peak load 100 €/MWh
Interruptible industry 10 % of the zone's peak load 3,000 €/MWh
